stops.name: Erfurt: Voilà un homme, the meeting with Goethe
stops.campa: At the Congress of princes he has summoned to Erfurt to overawe his ally the Tsar, Napoleon takes an hour from kings to receive the German poet whose Werther he has read seven times and carried through Egypt. He studies Goethe and pronounces, before witnesses, the sentence that will outlive most of the treaties signed that week, "there is a man," then turns the talk to tragedy, faults the drama of fate as belonging to a darker age, and urges him to write of Caesar instead. He leaves Goethe the cross of the Legion of Honor, still master of every crowned head in the room.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Goethe at Erfurt, 2 October 1808 (as Goethe records it)

stops.name: Wagram, the hundred-gun battery
stops.campa: On the marshy plain of Wagram, north of Vienna, in the second and decisive day of battle against the Archduke Charles, Napoleon masses Macdonald's massive infantry column and a battery of a hundred guns under Lauriston in the center, the largest concentration of artillery the wars have yet seen, and blasts a gap through the Austrian line. It is a costlier, cruder victory than Austerlitz: over thirty thousand French casualties in two days, but it forces Austria's fifth and last war against him to an end at the peace of Schönbrunn, clearing, at ruinous cost, the ground for the dynastic marriage he has already begun to plan.

stops.name: Paris, divorce from Joséphine
stops.campa: In the small salon of the Tuileries, before the assembled family, Napoleon reads a prepared statement dissolving fourteen years of marriage for reasons of state alone: Joséphine has given him love and years of happiness, he says, but no heir, and the Empire he has built needs a womb of undisputed royal blood to outlast him. Joséphine, weeping, tries to read her own reply and cannot finish it; he embraces her before the room. She keeps the title of Empress, the château of Malmaison, and his continuing, oddly tender letters, but the throne beside him is already being measured for an Austrian archduchess.
stops.quote: The interest of France... the good of the state, which desires that I leave behind me children who inherit my love for my people, requires that I renounce henceforth the sweetest connections of my life.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's statement of divorce, read to the imperial family, 15 December 1809

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Marie-Louise
stops.campa: Married by proxy in Vienna to an Austrian archduchess he has never met, a niece by marriage of blood to the Marie-Antoinette whose fall he witnessed as a cadet in the Paris crowds, Napoleon receives his eighteen-year-old bride at Compiègne and, by his own account, cannot wait for the religious ceremony to consummate the match. The public wedding, in the Salon Carré of the Louvre transformed into a chapel, seats every crowned head and ambassador he can summon; the House of Habsburg he once studied from the outside as a rival empire now supplies, by treaty of the bedchamber, the legitimacy his own crown was still missing.

stops.name: Paris, birth of the King of Rome
stops.campa: After a labor so dangerous the doctor Dubois is authorized, if it comes to a choice, to save the mother over the child, Marie-Louise delivers a son at the Tuileries. The cannon salute is arranged in advance to announce the sex: twenty-one shots for a daughter, a hundred and one for a son, and all Paris counts with the guns; at the twenty-second the whole city erupts before the salute is even finished. Napoleon carries the infant himself to the doors of the state apartments, presents him to the assembled grandees of the Empire with four words, and gives him, by decree already prepared, the title no Bonaparte has ever held: King of Rome.
stops.quote: Here is the King of Rome.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon presenting his newborn son, 20 March 1811 (period court memoirs)

stops.name: Moscow, entry and the fire
stops.campa: After Borodino's slaughter, the bloodiest single day the wars have yet produced, the Grande Armée enters an undefended, half-emptied Moscow, and Napoleon takes the Kremlin, "I am at length, then, in Moscow, in the ancient city of the Tsars," expecting Alexander's surrender within days. Instead the governor Rostopchin has seeded the city with incendiaries; that night fires break out across Moscow and within days more than two-thirds of the wooden capital burns to ash around the French garrison, lighting the Kremlin walls red by night. Napoleon watches from a window and calls it the most magnificent and frightening sight mankind has ever seen; the surrender he waited for never comes.
stops.quote: What resoluteness! What people! These are Scythians!
stops.quote_source: Napoleon, on learning Moscow's own governor had ordered the city burned, September 1812 (recorded by Ségur and other memoirists)

stops.name: Berezina, the crossing
stops.campa: Five weeks into the retreat from a Moscow that gave him ashes instead of peace, the wreck of the Grande Armée, starved, frostbitten, shadowed by Cossacks, finds the Berezina unfrozen and both banks held by converging Russian armies. General Éblé's pontonniers stand chest-deep in the freezing current for hours, building two trestle bridges under fire, and hold the crossing open two full days while a hundred thousand men, camp-followers, and guns funnel across; when the bridges are finally burned behind the rearguard, thousands still on the wrong bank are lost. The army that crossed the Niemen in June is, by the time it reaches Poland, a scattered fraction of itself.

stops.name: Leipzig, the Battle of the Nations
stops.campa: Half a million men, French against the combined armies of Austria, Prussia, Russia and Sweden, meet at Leipzig in the largest battle Europe has yet fought, four days of slaughter that cost some hundred and thirty thousand casualties before Napoleon, his Saxon allies deserting on the field itself, orders retreat across the single bridge over the Elster. A panicking corporal blows the bridge too soon, with thirty thousand French rearguard still on the wrong side; among the drowned is the Polish marshal Poniatowski, made marshal only days before. It is the Empire's largest defeat yet, and the war rolls, for the first time since 1794, onto French soil.

stops.name: Fontainebleau, farewell to the Old Guard
stops.campa: In the Cour du Cheval-Blanc at Fontainebleau, having failed a night before to end his own life with a phial of poison carried since Russia, Napoleon comes down the horseshoe staircase to say goodbye to the men who followed the eagles for twenty years. He kisses the tricolor of the Old Guard's standard, embraces General Petit, and tells the ranked grenadiers, most of them weeping openly, some fainting in the ranks, that he goes for the good of France, to spare her a civil war his own continuance would prolong. The Allies have already voted him the tiny island of Elba as sovereign; the Bourbons return to a throne he leaves them.
stops.quote: Soldiers of my Old Guard, I bid you farewell. For twenty years you have been my constant companions on the road to honour and glory... I could not embrace you all, but I embrace your general. Come, General Petit, let me press you to my heart.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's farewell to the Old Guard, Fontainebleau, 20 April 1814

stops.name: Elba, exile
stops.campa: Sovereign now of nothing but a Mediterranean island eighteen miles long, granted by the Allies as a face-saving cage, Napoleon governs Elba as if it were an empire in miniature: he reorganizes its mines, its roads, its tiny army of four hundred, redesigns his gardens at the Palazzina dei Mulini, and receives his mother and his sister Pauline while Joséphine, whom he still writes of with feeling, dies at Malmaison without his knowing until after. He reads the Vienna newspapers that reach him late, watches the Bourbon restoration mishandle a France already restless, and counts, from his window over the sea, the days until the money the treaty promised him stops arriving.

stops.name: Golfe-Juan, the flight of the eagle
stops.campa: With six hundred men of his Elba garrison packed onto a handful of small ships, Napoleon slips past the British watch and lands, without a shot fired, on the beach at Golfe-Juan between Cannes and Antibes. He avoids royalist Provence and strikes north through the mountains toward Grenoble, issuing along the road the proclamation drafted on shipboard, promising his soldiers that the eagle, with the national colors, will fly from steeple to steeple all the way to the towers of Notre-Dame. Near Laffrey a royal battalion blocks the pass; he walks alone toward their muskets, opens his coat, and dares them to fire on their Emperor. They break ranks and cheer him instead.
stops.quote: Soldiers! ... The eagle, with the national colours, will fly from steeple to steeple, all the way to the towers of Notre-Dame.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's proclamation to the army, 1 March 1815

stops.name: Waterloo, the last battle
stops.campa: On the muddy ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean, having failed to crush the Prussians decisively at Ligny two days before, Napoleon delays his main attack until the ground dries and gives Blücher's army the hours it needs to march to Wellington's aid. Ney's cavalry breaks itself for hours against unbroken British squares; the Imperial Guard, sent forward at last in the evening as the final reserve of twenty years of war, is thrown back for the first time in its history, and the cry that the Guard recoils breaks the whole army's nerve. Napoleon is swept from the field in the general rout, his last throw of everything spent by nightfall against Wellington and the Prussians together.
stops.quote: The Guard recoils... All is lost.
stops.quote_source: Cries reported through the French ranks as the Imperial Guard broke, evening of 18 June 1815 (period accounts of the rout)
